title: Grainstack, Evening
subject: A golden field with a purple grainstack beneath a warm evening sky.

painter_words:
I've left **Grainstack, Evening** as it was at day 415. I painted nothing this sitting. I looked at the whole canvas in normal colour, in squint and gallery light, and in close crops of every passage I'd flagged before. Nothing needed another hand.

The picture is still one evening chord. A big straw stack stands in violet shadow with a hot orange rim on its right side. Its ragged shadow runs across gold stubble, and a smaller stack echoes it in the distance. The sky goes from cerulean through rose to lemon, with a pale sun resting on hazy poplars. In the blurred squint view the light and dark masses hold up well. The dark stack and its shadow stand clearly against the bright band of sky and the gold field.

**Accepted as they are:**
- **Haze right of the sun:** the hard step I fixed last time is gone. A faint ochre smudge near the sun shows in close-up but not at full size. Earlier attempts in that narrow band only made it worse.
- **Gold flecks in the poplars:** faint up close; at full size the trees read as solid violet.
- **Broad far end of the cast shadow:** it anchors the lower-left corner.
- **Distant stack:** fine. It sits in the stubble with its rim lit.

**Thought about but left alone:** more glow around the sun. Glazes in small areas have pooled into blots every time, and a soft, low-contrast sun suits a hazy evening.

My heart is happy with this, and I don't feel a pull to take anything further.

**Handoff:** everything is dry at day 415. The journal has the full notes, and the lessons from last time still apply:
- To get rid of a seam or break up a hard-edged mass, paint over dry paint with ragged-edged strokes of the neighbouring colours.
- Blend at most one pass, and never over a fresh, sparse hatch.
- A spirits rag lifts wet paint back to the dry layer underneath, but leaves a faint streak where each wipe ends.
- To match or cover a passage, re-mix its recipe from the log.
- Try new marks small first, and lift them if they fail.
- After working near a finished dry outline, wipe inside it while the new paint is wet.
- To flatten dry thick paint, use a runny coat of the same colour, not a knife.

These are still hypotheses:
- Glazes in narrow bands pool.
- Two runny coats level better than one.
- Marks spaced evenly along a line read as a fence.
- A light rag wipe does little to normally loaded strokes.

painter_words:
**October Dusk, the River Meadow**

The painting is finished, and I'm content with it. It shows a river meadow about twenty minutes after sunset. A lemon glow fades upward into violet-gray, and the pale pond below catches the same light. A dark grove of elms stands on the right, with the glow showing under its canopy between the trunks. A hazy far tree line runs behind the water, with a farmhouse and a thread of smoke. A small woman in a red shawl walks the worn path down toward the water. She is the one warm note in the picture and gives it its scale.

This visit was short:
- **Right-hand tree:** I took the pale streaks out and stippled a little dark over the dry paint, so the tree now reads as quiet shadow.
- **Left meadow:** I tried an opaque olive band near the shore, and it went down as a flat patch. It took many passes with a rag dipped in spirits to lift it, and a slight warm tint is left over the texture. This is the third time opaque paint over the textured meadow has turned into a patch; only transparent glazes work there.
- **Final glaze:** A graded transparent glaze darkens the left meadow from the shore toward the foreground. The field now rolls down into shadow, and the lit ground stays by the water and around the figure.

The crown edges are still more scalloped than Inness would have left them. Still, the glow caught twice, in the sky and in the water, with the dark trees between, is the place I set out to paint. My reflections are in the journal.

painter_words:
**"Evening on the Upland Lake"** (72 × 56 cm, oil on linen)

This session I went back to the one passage my last notes called weak — the far shore — and rebuilt it. The line of reeds that had been a comb is now a low broken band of wood along the far waterline, clumped and gapped, with seven bare trees standing out of it at uneven intervals; mist swallows its base and its right-hand end. Under it, in the water, is the shore's own dark grain reflected as a soft continuous band.

What it cost: two lozenge disasters that each took four days of drying and a full cover with mist paint before I could repair them. The lesson is mechanical and I have written it down — a "body" stroke is 20–60 units long, and when my masks were 90 units wide and 12 tall, one stroke covered the whole shape and its outline became the mark. Small strokes over small shapes, then merged while wet with a clean soft brush, is what actually builds a reflection.

I also spent time nearly repainting a pale streak on the right that I took for scum on the lake; measured against a grid it turned out to be the lit crest of the near bank, and I left it alone.

Left standing: the near trees' limbs are still bars at arm's length, and the bank is still empty through the middle. Both have been corrected three times now and both got worse each time.
